claim: Medaka (Oryzias latipes species complex) is a small, egg-laying freshwater fish from East Asia.
source: Medaka (Oryzias latipes species complex) is a small, egg-laying freshwater fish from East Asia (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about medaka that is directly stated in the manuscript and supported by established knowledge about the organism.

claim: Medaka is often found in rice fields.
source: It is often found in rice fields, which earned it its common English name of ricefish and the genus name of Oryzias (based on the genus name of rice, Oryza).
evidence: This is a direct statement about medaka's habitat that is presented as established knowledge.

claim: The medaka has been kept as an ornamental fish in Japan from as early as the 17th century.
source: The medaka has been kept as an ornamental fish in Japan from as early as the 17th century, and its central role in Japanese culture is exemplified by its appearance in pieces ranging from Edo era paintings (Kinoshita et al., 2009; Naruse et al., 2011; Takeda and Shimada, 2010) to modern-day children's songs (Mamun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature documenting the historical and cultural significance of medaka.

claim: Medaka was reclassified in the genus Oryzias by Jordan and Snyder in 1906 to become Oryzias latipes.
source: It was reclassified in the genus Oryzias by Jordan and Snyder (1906) to become Oryzias latipes, and, more recently, it has become clear that the medaka comprises a species complex rather that a single species (Table 1).
evidence: This is a historical taxonomic fact supported by citation to the reclassification work.

claim: The medaka comprises a species complex rather than a single species.
source: It was reclassified in the genus Oryzias by Jordan and Snyder (1906) to become Oryzias latipes, and, more recently, it has become clear that the medaka comprises a species complex rather that a single species (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Table 1 which shows multiple species within the complex, representing an inference from accumulated data.

claim: Males of Oryzias latipes can be easily distinguished from females by their elongated anal and dorsal fins.
source: Males can be easily distinguished from females by their elongated anal and dorsal fins.
evidence: This claim is stated in the figure caption and is observable in Figure 1A showing male and female medaka.

claim: Medaka proved to be an ideal laboratory organism that was easy to maintain due to its small body size, and its simple dietary and habitat requirements.
source: It later proved to be an ideal laboratory organism that was easy to maintain due to its small body size, and its simple dietary and habitat requirements.
evidence: This is a statement about medaka's suitability as a model organism based on established knowledge from decades of laboratory use.

claim: Medaka has a comparably small genome size of approximately 700 Mb.
source: The combination of a sexual dimorphism, short generation times, large and transparent eggs with easily observable development, high tolerance to inbreeding and a comparably small genome size (~700 Mb) also made medaka suitable for a wide range of studies (Braasch et al., 2015; Kasahara et al., 2007; Kirchmaier et al., 2015; Parenti, 2008; Wittbrodt et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a specific measurement of genome size supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Early systematic crossing of color mutants of medaka provided evidence for Mendelian inheritance in vertebrates.
source: Early systematic crossing of color mutants of medaka provided evidence for Mendelian inheritance in vertebrates, sex limited inheritance and crossing over between sex chromosomes (Aida, 1921; Ishikawa, 1913; Toyama, 1916).
evidence: This historical scientific finding is supported by citations to early 20th century research papers.

claim: The first hormone induced sex-reversal was achieved in medaka by Yamamoto in 1958.
source: Subsequently, the first hormone induced sex-reversal (Yamamoto, 1958) and the discovery of the first sex determining gene in a non-mammalian vertebrate (Matsuda et al., 2002) paved the way for the medaka as a model for sex determination and sex differentiation (Kondo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a historical scientific achievement supported by citation to the original work.

claim: The first sex determining gene in a non-mammalian vertebrate was discovered in medaka.
source: Subsequently, the first hormone induced sex-reversal (Yamamoto, 1958) and the discovery of the first sex determining gene in a non-mammalian vertebrate (Matsuda et al., 2002) paved the way for the medaka as a model for sex determination and sex differentiation (Kondo et al., 2009).
evidence: This scientific milestone is supported by citation to the discovery paper.

claim: The first active DNA-based transposable element (Tol1) in a vertebrate was detected in medaka.
source: Scientific milestones achieved with the medaka further include the detection of the first active DNA-based transposable element (Tol1) in a vertebrate (Koga et al., 1995), which laid the foundation for the development of several tools for genetic modification (Koga, 2011).
evidence: This scientific discovery is supported by citation to the original detection paper.

claim: Medaka's genome became available as one of the first for any vertebrate.
source: Medaka's role as genomic model organism was consolidated when its genome became available as one of the first for any vertebrate (Kasahara et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement about genome sequencing is supported by citation to the genome publication.

claim: The gene-editing tool CRISPR/Cas9 was established in medaka and employed in multiple studies.
source: More recently, the gene-editing tool CRISPR/Cas9 was also established in medaka and employed in multiple studies (e.g. Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018; Letelier et al., 2018; Murakami et al., 2017; Watakabe et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim about the application of CRISPR/Cas9 technology is supported by citations to multiple studies using this tool.

claim: Medaka serves as a complementary model to zebrafish in many fields, including cancer research.
source: In many fields, including cancer research, medaka serves as complementary model to the well-established zebrafish (Schartl and Walter, 2016; Takeda and Shimada, 2010).
evidence: This statement about medaka's role relative to zebrafish is supported by citations to review literature.

claim: Medaka species are distributed in Japan, China, Taiwan and Korea.
source: Medaka species are distributed in Japan, China, Taiwan and Korea (Shima and Mitani, 2004; Yamamoto, 1975), where they are mainly found in standing and slow-flowing water bodies such as rice paddies, ponds and agricultural channels (Fukuda et al., 2005, Figure 1B).
evidence: This geographic distribution is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Medaka are mainly found in standing and slow-flowing water bodies such as rice paddies, ponds and agricultural channels.
source: Medaka species are distributed in Japan, China, Taiwan and Korea (Shima and Mitani, 2004; Yamamoto, 1975), where they are mainly found in standing and slow-flowing water bodies such as rice paddies, ponds and agricultural channels (Fukuda et al., 2005, Figure 1B).
evidence: This habitat description is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1B showing medaka in their natural habitat.

claim: The preferred habitats of medaka are shallow zones close to the shoreline with abundant plant cover.
source: The preferred habitats of medaka are shallow zones close to the shoreline with abundant plant cover where it feeds on microscopic organisms, including algae and zooplankton (Edeline et al., 2016; Fukuda et al., 2005).
evidence: This habitat preference is supported by citations to observational studies.

claim: Medaka feeds on microscopic organisms, including algae and zooplankton.
source: The preferred habitats of medaka are shallow zones close to the shoreline with abundant plant cover where it feeds on microscopic organisms, including algae and zooplankton (Edeline et al., 2016; Fukuda et al., 2005).
evidence: This dietary information is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Medaka is likely mainly preyed upon by dragonfly larvae, birds and predatory fishes.
source: Although detailed studies on its position in the food web are lacking, medaka is likely mainly preyed upon by dragonfly larvae, birds and predatory fishes.
evidence: This is stated as a likelihood based on inference from general ecological knowledge, with the caveat that detailed studies are lacking.

claim: Throughout its life, medaka is parasitized by both ectoparasites and endoparasites from across the animal kingdom.
source: Throughout its life, medaka is parasitized by both ectoparasites and endoparasites from across the animal kingdom (catalogued in: Nagasawa, 2017), and females appear to be particularly susceptible to ectoparasites during the breeding season (Edeline et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim about parasitism is supported by citation to a catalogue of parasites.

claim: Female medaka appear to be particularly susceptible to ectoparasites during the breeding season.
source: Throughout its life, medaka is parasitized by both ectoparasites and endoparasites from across the animal kingdom (catalogued in: Nagasawa, 2017), and females appear to be particularly susceptible to ectoparasites during the breeding season (Edeline et al., 2016).
evidence: This observation about sex-specific parasite susceptibility is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: In the wild, most medaka have a lifespan of roughly one year.
source: In the wild, most medaka have a lifespan of roughly one year during which males and females can reach a length between three and four centimeters (Leaf et al., 2011; Parenti, 2008; Shima and Mitani, 2004; Yamamoto, 1975).
evidence: This lifespan estimate is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Male and female medaka can reach a length between three and four centimeters.
source: In the wild, most medaka have a lifespan of roughly one year during which males and females can reach a length between three and four centimeters (Leaf et al., 2011; Parenti, 2008; Shima and Mitani, 2004; Yamamoto, 1975).
evidence: This size range is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: In captivity, medaka may live for more than four years.
source: In captivity, medaka may live for more than four years (Egami and Etoh, 1969).
evidence: This observation about captive lifespan is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Medaka tolerates a wide range of temperatures, from 4°C to 40°C.
source: As an inhabitant of the temperate zone, medaka is confronted with and tolerates a wide range of temperatures, from 4°C to 40°C (Kinoshita et al., 2009; Sampetrean et al., 2009).
evidence: This temperature tolerance range is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: When the water cools down, medaka fish enter a state of hibernation during which they barely move and stop feeding.
source: When the water cools down, fish enter a state of hibernation during which they barely move and stop feeding (Edeline et al., 2016; Kinoshita et al., 2009).
evidence: This behavioral response to cold is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Cooling has been used in the lab to slow down the life cycle of medaka and store it for later use.
source: Cooling has been used in the lab to slow down the life cycle of medaka and store it for later use (Wittbrodt et al., 2002).
evidence: This laboratory practice is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: During the breeding season, medaka spawns every morning around sunrise.
source: During the breeding season, medaka spawns every morning around sunrise (Leaf et al., 2011; Ueda and Oishi, 1982).
evidence: This spawning behavior is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Mating in medaka involves an intricate courtship dance during which males repeatedly approach females and exhibit diverse displays.
source: Mating involves an intricate courtship dance during which males repeatedly approach females and exhibit diverse displays (Ono and Uematsu, 1957).
evidence: This courtship behavior is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: If accepted, male medaka hold on to the females with their elongated anal and dorsal fins, while females spawn up to 48 eggs.
source: If accepted, males hold on to the females with their elongated anal and dorsal fins, while females spawn up to 48 eggs (Leaf et al., 2011).
evidence: This mating behavior and egg number is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Bundles of fertilized medaka eggs stay attached to the mother's ovarian cavity via attaching filaments for up to a few hours, before they are deposited.
source: Bundles of fertilized eggs stay attached to the mother's ovarian cavity via attaching filaments for up to a few hours, before they are deposited (Parenti, 2005).
evidence: This reproductive behavior is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The reasons for the evolution of the unusual reproductive strategy of egg attachment in medaka remain unexplored.
source: Despite its practical use in the laboratory to easily harvest eggs from unambiguously identifiable mothers, the reasons for the evolution of this unusual reproductive strategy remain unexplored.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about a gap in knowledge regarding the evolutionary basis of this trait.

claim: Medaka juveniles hatch after 7–9 days.
source: Juveniles finally hatch after 7–9 days and grow to maturity within about two and a half months (Iwamatsu, 2004; Takeda and Shimada, 2010).
evidence: This developmental timing is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Medaka juveniles grow to maturity within about two and a half months.
source: Juveniles finally hatch after 7–9 days and grow to maturity within about two and a half months (Iwamatsu, 2004; Takeda and Shimada, 2010).
evidence: This developmental timing is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Relatively little of our current knowledge on the biology of medaka has been gathered from studies in the wild.
source: Overall, relatively little of our current knowledge on the biology of medaka has been gathered from studies in the wild.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of knowledge based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: Differences between Japanese medaka populations were recognized early on.
source: Differences between Japanese medaka populations were recognized early on (Sakaizumi, 1984), but it is only now that the scientific community has begun to fully appreciate the diversity summarized within the "medaka".
evidence: This historical observation is supported by citation to an early study.

claim: The northern and southern Japanese populations were regarded as a single species, Oryzias latipes, for a long time.
source: For a long time, the so-called northern and southern Japanese populations, from which the two most famous medaka inbred lines (Hd-rR and HNI) are derived, were regarded as a single species: Oryzias latipes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statement about historical taxonomic treatment supported by reference to Figure 1C showing the locations of these strains.

claim: The northern Japanese population was described as a new species, Oryzias sakaizumii, by Asai et al. in 2011.
source: Hence, the northern Japanese population was described as a new species: Oryzias sakaizumii by Asai et al., 2011, and medaka is now frequently referred to as "Oryzias latipes species complex" (Iguchi et al., 2018; Kawajiri et al., 2015; Takehana et al., 2016).
evidence: This taxonomic description is supported by citation to the original species description.

claim: Oryzias latipes and Oryzias sakaizumii were estimated to have diverged between 3 and 8 million years ago.
source: Depending on the method, Oryzias latipes and Oryzias sakaizumii were estimated to have diverged between 3 and 8 million years ago (Figure 2A, Katsumura et al., 2019; Takehana et al., 2003; but see Setiamarga et al., 2009).
evidence: This divergence time estimate is supported by citations to published studies and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Oryzias latipes and Oryzias sakaizumii differ in craniofacial anatomy.
source: They differ in a number of traits including craniofacial anatomy (Kimura et al., 2007), body coloration (Asai et al., 2011), aggressiveness (Kagawa, 2014) and the degree of sexual dimorphism of the dorsal fin (Asai et al., 2011), the last of which is likely mediated by different sex steroid levels during development (Katsumura et al., 2014; Kawajiri et al., 2015).
evidence: This morphological difference is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Oryzias latipes and Oryzias sakaizumii differ in body coloration.
source: They differ in a number of traits including craniofacial anatomy (Kimura et al., 2007), body coloration (Asai et al., 2011), aggressiveness (Kagawa, 2014) and the degree of sexual dimorphism of the dorsal fin (Asai et al., 2011), the last of which is likely mediated by different sex steroid levels during development (Katsumura et al., 2014; Kawajiri et al., 2015).
evidence: This difference in coloration is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Oryzias latipes and Oryzias sakaizumii differ in aggressiveness.
source: They differ in a number of traits including craniofacial anatomy (Kimura et al., 2007), body coloration (Asai et al., 2011), aggressiveness (Kagawa, 2014) and the degree of sexual dimorphism of the dorsal fin (Asai et al., 2011), the last of which is likely mediated by different sex steroid levels during development (Katsumura et al., 2014; Kawajiri et al., 2015).
evidence: This behavioral difference is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Oryzias latipes and Oryzias sakaizumii differ in the degree of sexual dimorphism of the dorsal fin.
source: They differ in a number of traits including craniofacial anatomy (Kimura et al., 2007), body coloration (Asai et al., 2011), aggressiveness (Kagawa, 2014) and the degree of sexual dimorphism of the dorsal fin (Asai et al., 2011), the last of which is likely mediated by different sex steroid levels during development (Katsumura et al., 2014; Kawajiri et al., 2015).
evidence: This morphological difference is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The difference in sexual dimorphism of the dorsal fin between Oryzias latipes and Oryzias sakaizumii is likely mediated by different sex steroid levels during development.
source: They differ in a number of traits including craniofacial anatomy (Kimura et al., 2007), body coloration (Asai et al., 2011), aggressiveness (Kagawa, 2014) and the degree of sexual dimorphism of the dorsal fin (Asai et al., 2011), the last of which is likely mediated by different sex steroid levels during development (Katsumura et al., 2014; Kawajiri et al., 2015).
evidence: This mechanistic explanation is supported by citations to published studies and is stated as likely, indicating inference.

claim: Oryzias latipes and O. sakaizumii produce viable hybrid offspring in the laboratory.
source: Nonetheless, both species produce viable hybrid offspring in the laboratory (e.g. Murata et al., 2012) and current evidence also suggests limited gene flow in the wild (Iguchi et al., 2018; Katsumura et al., 2019).
evidence: This observation about hybridization is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Current evidence suggests limited gene flow between Oryzias latipes and O. sakaizumii in the wild.
source: Nonetheless, both species produce viable hybrid offspring in the laboratory (e.g. Murata et al., 2012) and current evidence also suggests limited gene flow in the wild (Iguchi et al., 2018; Katsumura et al., 2019).
evidence: This inference about gene flow is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Oryzias latipes colonized the main island of Japan from the south (i.e., from Kyushu) and subsequently dispersed along the Pacific coast.
source: Recent insight into the biogeography of the medaka also suggests that O. latipes colonized the main island of Japan from the south (i.e., from Kyushu) and subsequently dispersed along the Pacific coast (Katsumura et al., 2019).
evidence: This biogeographic inference is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Oryzias sakaizumii likely originated on the western side of the Japanese Alps.
source: In contrast, Oryzias sakaizumii likely originated on the western side of the Japanese Alps, which still largely separate both species in their current distribution (Figure 2A, Katsumura et al., 2019).
evidence: This biogeographic inference is supported by citation to a study and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Japanese Alps still largely separate Oryzias latipes and O. sakaizumii in their current distribution.
source: In contrast, Oryzias sakaizumii likely originated on the western side of the Japanese Alps, which still largely separate both species in their current distribution (Figure 2A, Katsumura et al., 2019).
evidence: This geographic separation is supported by citation and shown in Figure 2A distribution maps.

claim: The Korean medaka lineages are genetically divergent from the Japanese species and also highly structured.
source: The Korean medaka lineages are genetically divergent from the Japanese species and also highly structured (Figures 1C and 2A).
evidence: This genetic divergence is stated and supported by reference to figures showing phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Korean medaka lineages comprise at least two subgroups referred to as the East Korean (HSOK strain) and China–West Korean populations.
source: They comprise at least two subgroups that have been referred to as the East Korean (HSOK strain) and China–West Korean populations (Ds et al., 2013; Kang et al., 2005; Katsumura et al., 2019; Parenti, 2008).
evidence: This population structure is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: The China–West Korean population together with populations from Taiwan likely represents a different species: Oryzias sinensis.
source: Although still frequently referred to as O. latipes (see Katsumura et al., 2019; Spivakov et al., 2014; Takeda and Shimada, 2010), the China–West Korean population together with populations from Taiwan, likely represents a different species: Oryzias sinensis (see Ds et al., 2013; Parenti, 2008; Tzeng et al., 2006).
evidence: This taxonomic inference is supported by citations to published studies and is stated as likely.

claim: Mitochondrial phylogenies indicate the existence of a locally restricted ancient Taiwanese medaka lineage and two lineages derived from more recent invasion events.
source: While further data are required, mitochondrial phylogenies indicate the existence of a locally restricted ancient Taiwanese medaka lineage and two lineages derived from more recent invasion events (Tzeng et al., 2006).
evidence: This phylogenetic inference is supported by citation to a published study, with the caveat that further data are needed.

claim: Continental O. sinensis are genetically diverse and geographically distant populations exhibit signatures of divergence.
source: Continental O. sinensis are also genetically diverse and geographically distant populations exhibit signatures of divergence, for example, between Shanghai and Korea (Katsumura et al., 2019).
evidence: This genetic diversity is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Comprehensive studies covering the morphological and genetic diversity in continental Asia are still lacking.
source: However, comprehensive studies covering the morphological and genetic diversity in continental Asia are still lacking.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about a gap in current knowledge.

claim: A recent study identified differences in courtship between populations of O. sakaizumii, which were inferred to result from stronger sexual selection at lower latitudes.
source: For example, a recent study identified differences in courtship between populations of O. sakaizumii, which were inferred to result from stronger sexual selection at lower latitudes (Sasaki and Yamahira, 2016).
evidence: This finding about courtship variation and its interpretation is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Juveniles of O. sakaizumii from higher latitudes compensate for a shorter growing season further north with faster growth rates.
source: Additionally, juveniles of O. sakaizumii from higher latitudes compensate for a shorter growing season further north with faster growth rates (Yamahira and Takeshi, 2008).
evidence: This adaptive pattern is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Faster growth in O. sakaizumii, which is achieved by higher feeding rates, comes with a cost and is accompanied by higher vulnerability for predation by dragonfly larvae.
source: However, faster growth, which is achieved by higher feeding rates, comes with a cost and is accompanied by higher vulnerability for predation by dragonfly larvae (Suzuki et al., 2010).
evidence: This trade-off between growth and predation risk is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Different growth capacities in O. sakaizumii likely evolve in response to both predation pressure and length of the growing season.
source: Hence, different growth capacities in O. sakaizumii likely evolve in response to both predation pressure and length of the growing season (Suzuki et al., 2010).
evidence: This evolutionary interpretation is supported by citation and is stated as likely, indicating inference.

claim: Ricefishes comprise 36 described species in two genera (Oryzias: 32 species, Adrianichthys: four species).
source: Although mainly recognized for medaka, ricefishes comprise a considerable diversity with 36 described species in two genera (Oryzias: 32 species, Adrianichthys: four species, Asai et al., 2011; Herder et al., 2012a; Herder and Chapuis, 2010; Magtoon, 2010; Mandagi et al., 2018; Mokodongan et al., 2014; Parenti, 2008; Parenti et al., 2013; Parenti and Hadiaty, 2010).
evidence: This taxonomic count is supported by citations to multiple taxonomic publications.

claim: Ricefishes form three major clades referred to as the latipes-, javanicus- and celebensis species group.
source: They form three major clades referred to as the latipes-, javanicus- and celebensis species group, the last of which diversified on Sulawesi, Indonesia (Figure 2A, Mokodongan and Yamahira, 2015; Takehana et al., 2005).
evidence: This phylogenetic structure is supported by citations and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The celebensis species group diversified on Sulawesi, Indonesia.
source: They form three major clades referred to as the latipes-, javanicus- and celebensis species group, the last of which diversified on Sulawesi, Indonesia (Figure 2A, Mokodongan and Yamahira, 2015; Takehana et al., 2005).
evidence: This biogeographic pattern is supported by citations and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sulawesi has a total of 21 ricefish species and 19 local endemics, making it a hotspot of ricefish diversity.
source: With a total of 21 species and 19 local endemics, this island represents a hotspot of ricefish diversity (Figures 1C and 2A–B).
evidence: This diversity count is stated and supported by reference to figures showing distribution and species counts.

claim: Nine newly described ricefish species within the last decade, eight of them endemic to Sulawesi, suggest that both the global ricefish biodiversity as well as the ricefish fauna of Sulawesi are still underdescribed.
source: Additionally, nine newly described species within the last decade, eight of them endemic to Sulawesi, suggest that both the global ricefish biodiversity as well as the ricefish fauna of Sulawesi are still underdescribed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This inference about underdescribed diversity is based on the recent rate of species descriptions shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Seven sex chromosomes and three different master sex determination genes have been identified in ricefish species.
source: So far, seven sex chromosomes and three different master SD genes have been identified in ricefish species (Figure 2A).
evidence: This count of sex determination systems is stated and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: O. latipes has a young XY system in which dmrt1bY (dmy) on linkage group 1 (LG1) acts as the male sex determination gene.
source: For example, O. latipes has a young XY system in which dmrt1bY (dmy) on linkage group 1 (LG1) acts as the male SD gene (Matsuda, 2005; Matsuda et al., 2002).
evidence: This sex determination mechanism is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In O. luzonensis, gsdf on LG12 is the sex determination gene.
source: In contrast, gsdf on LG12 is the SD gene in O. luzonensis (Myosho et al., 2012), and sox3 on LG10 serves as SD gene in O. dancena, O. marmoratus and O. profundicola (Figure 2A, Myosho et al., 2015; Takehana et al., 2014).
evidence: This sex determination mechanism is supported by citation and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: sox3 on LG10 serves as sex determination gene in O. dancena, O. marmoratus and O. profundicola.
source: In contrast, gsdf on LG12 is the SD gene in O. luzonensis (Myosho et al., 2012), and sox3 on LG10 serves as SD gene in O. dancena, O. marmoratus and O. profundicola (Figure 2A, Myosho et al., 2015; Takehana et al., 2014).
evidence: This sex determination mechanism is supported by citations and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Oryzias hubbsi and O. javanicus exhibit a ZW (female heterogametic) system, albeit with different sex chromosomes.
source: Oryzias hubbsi and O. javanicus even exhibit a ZW, i.e. female heterogametic, system, albeit with different sex chromosomes (Takehana et al., 2007b).
evidence: This sex determination system is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Most Oryzias are primarily found in freshwater.
source: While most Oryzias are primarily found in freshwater, O. javanicus and O. dancena (also referred to as O. melastigma, likely a synonym; Parenti, 2008; Roberts, 1998) occur in saltwater and brackish water, respectively.
evidence: This habitat preference is stated as general knowledge with citations supporting the synonymy note.

claim: O. javanicus occurs in saltwater.
source: While most Oryzias are primarily found in freshwater, O. javanicus and O. dancena (also referred to as O. melastigma, likely a synonym; Parenti, 2008; Roberts, 1998) occur in saltwater and brackish water, respectively.
evidence: This habitat preference is stated as established knowledge.

claim: O. dancena occurs in brackish water.
source: While most Oryzias are primarily found in freshwater, O. javanicus and O. dancena (also referred to as O. melastigma, likely a synonym; Parenti, 2008; Roberts, 1998) occur in saltwater and brackish water, respectively.
evidence: This habitat preference is stated as established knowledge.

claim: O. javanicus and O. dancena are being established as models for marine ecotoxicology to complement the medaka's role in freshwater.
source: These species are being established as models for marine ecotoxicology to complement the medaka's role in freshwater (Chen et al., 2011; Dong et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2018; Koyama et al., 2008).
evidence: This emerging use as model organisms is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Oryzias latipes can better adjust to saltwater when exposed to elevated levels of salinity earlier in life.
source: Interestingly, Oryzias latipes can better adjust to saltwater when exposed to elevated levels of salinity earlier in life (Miyanishi et al., 2016).
evidence: This physiological observation is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Species from some remote freshwater systems in Indonesia do not tolerate even small changes in osmolarity.
source: In contrast, species from some remote freshwater systems in Indonesia do not tolerate even small changes in osmolarity (Inoue and Takei, 2002; Myosho et al., 2018).
evidence: This physiological observation is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Salinity tolerance in Oryzias is based on both genetic and epigenetic factors.
source: Salinity tolerance in Oryzias is based on both genetic (Myosho et al., 2018, Ogoshi et al., 2015) and epigenetic factors, including an increase in the density of osmoregulating cells called ionocytes (Liu et al., 2016; Miyanishi et al., 2016) and an increase in activity of the same cells (Kang et al., 2008).
evidence: This mechanistic explanation is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Epigenetic factors contributing to salinity tolerance in Oryzias include an increase in the density of osmoregulating cells called ionocytes.
source: Salinity tolerance in Oryzias is based on both genetic (Myosho et al., 2018, Ogoshi et al., 2015) and epigenetic factors, including an increase in the density of osmoregulating cells called ionocytes (Liu et al., 2016; Miyanishi et al., 2016) and an increase in activity of the same cells (Kang et al., 2008).
evidence: This physiological mechanism is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Epigenetic factors contributing to salinity tolerance in Oryzias include an increase in activity of ionocytes.
source: Salinity tolerance in Oryzias is based on both genetic (Myosho et al., 2018, Ogoshi et al., 2015) and epigenetic factors, including an increase in the density of osmoregulating cells called ionocytes (Liu et al., 2016; Miyanishi et al., 2016) and an increase in activity of the same cells (Kang et al., 2008).
evidence: This physiological mechanism is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: While most ricefishes are largely pale in color, Sulawesi ricefishes exhibit several different fin and nuptial colorations.
